title: Designing your practice
hookLine: a place, a cue, a tiny start and an inner reason: the habit days, gathered into one plan
last: SELF-COMPASSION AFTER A SLIP FUELS TRYING AGAIN.

cards: A carpenter doesn't build a bookshelf by staring at a pile of wood and hoping. There's a sketch first, a few lines on the back of an envelope: how tall, which wall, where the screws go.
The habit days have handed over a lot of wood. Habits live in places. A cue sets them off.
Tiny starts beat heroic ones. A reason of your own outlasts a prize. A slip can be met kindly.
On the last day of the week, the pieces become one sketch, small enough to fit on a sticky note.

teach.h: A PLACE: THIS CHAIR, THIS CORNER.
teach.b: The design has four parts, each from a day on this path. First, a place. The habit research kept finding that routines cling to settings: the same chair, the same corner, the same window.
Not "somewhere quiet". This chair. This step on the back porch.

teach.h: A CUE: WHEN THIS, THEN THAT.
teach.b: A habit needs a doorbell, and the when-then days put it plainly: when this happens, then I do that. After the kettle clicks, I sit. After I park the car, I take three breaths before opening the door.
The cue already happens every day, so the new thing can ride on it.
Third, a tiny start, small enough that a tired, distracted, grumpy version of you could still do it. One breath. One line read.
One minute. It can grow later; for now the job is making showing up nearly automatic.
Fourth, an inner reason. Not a reward, not a streak, not a score: a sentence that's yours. "Because I want to be less sharp with my kids."
"Because the mornings feel crowded." The research on motivation suggested that reasons from within tend to last longer than prizes from outside.

Long before any lab, the Stoic teacher Epictetus put it in a line, as George Long translated it: "Every habit and faculty is maintained and increased by the corresponding actions: the habit of walking by walking, the habit of running by running."
Design doesn't do the walking. It just makes the first step easy to find.

how: People building a regular practice often write a short plan naming the place, the cue that comes before it, a very small first step and their own reason, and keep it where they'll see it; Stoic teachers like Epictetus treated character as built by repeated action.

o: choosing the best method from a list of experts
a strict daily schedule with no room for slips
a short plan: place, cue, tiny start, own reason

s: a good design starts with a big, impressive goal
the design starts tiny: small enough that a tired, grumpy version of you could still do it.
a cue works best when it's something that already happens every day
the new practice rides on something that already happens, like the kettle clicking.
Epictetus said habits grow by thinking about them
he said each habit grows by its own actions: walking by walking, running by running.

games.q: you're writing your design. which line works best as the 'where'?
o: somewhere quiet, when I get the chance.
games.why: the design names an exact spot. habits cling to settings, so a real chair beats a vague wish.

practice: Fill in four short blanks, in your head or on paper: where, the exact spot; when, the cue that comes right before; what, a start so small it's almost silly; why, one honest sentence.
Read the four lines back once, then let them rest and sit with the breath for the time that's left.

wordCard.voice: Designing your practice. Four lines, a place, a cue, a tiny start and a reason of your own, so the practice has somewhere to live. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: my design. A sketch small enough for a sticky note is a sketch you can keep. Until tomorrow.
